status: Policy report and recommendations, not enacted law
title: Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, Part 1: Digital Replicas
finding: Recommends a federal digital-replica right and says licences should use informed consent, full disclosure of intended uses and limited terms.

status: Enacted, applicable to specified new performances fixed on or after January 1, 2025
title: AB 2602: Contracts against public policy, digital replicas
finding: Makes a covered contract provision unenforceable for specified new digital-replica performances when intended use is not reasonably specific and the individual lacks the representation described by the statute.

title: AB 1836: Use of likeness, digital replica
finding: Adds liability for producing, distributing or making available certain unauthorized digital replicas of deceased personalities in expressive works, subject to listed exceptions.

title: ELVIS Act, Public Chapter 588
finding: Adds voice, including a readily identifiable simulation, to Tennessee’s protected personal rights and extends liability to specified unauthorized uses and distribution.

status: Advanced by the Senate Judiciary Committee by voice vote on June 18, 2026; a September 30 unanimous-consent request was blocked; not enacted as of October 13, 2026
title: S.4591: NO FAKES Act of 2026
finding: Would create a federal right in an individual’s voice and visual likeness, with a notice-and-counter-notice framework and enumerated speech protections. It remains proposed legislation.

status: Enacted as Public Law 119-12; the covered-platform notice-and-removal requirement took effect May 19, 2026
title: TAKE IT DOWN Act, Public Law 119-12
finding: Creates a narrow federal rule for nonconsensual intimate depictions, including defined digital forgeries, and requires covered platforms to operate a notice-and-removal process. It is not a general commercial likeness-licensing statute.

title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 50
finding: Requires certain providers to mark synthetic outputs in a machine-readable and detectable format and certain deployers to disclose deepfake image, audio or video, subject to the regulation’s exceptions.

status: Government report with a separate digital-replicas consultation announced
title: Report on Copyright and Artificial Intelligence
finding: Says replicas can imitate a person’s voice or likeness without permission, identifies gaps in existing protection and announces further consultation rather than a completed licensing rule.

title: Artificial Intelligence under the 2025 Commercials Contract
finding: Describes consent for creation and use, a separate clear writing, reasonably specific intended use, added consent beyond scope, compensation, access security and storage limits.

jurisdiction: Covered United States television and theatrical work
status: Collective agreement with some phased provisions
title: 2026 Theatrical and Television Memorandum of Agreement
finding: Addresses consent, payment, legitimate-business-need access, security, transfer obligations and use-specific treatment for digital replicas, with some terms phased to later dates.

title: Interactive Digital Replicas and Consent
finding: Describes separate written consent, a reasonably specific intended use, per-game compensation and rules allowing performers to suspend consent for generating new material during a strike.

title: FTC Endorsement Guides: What People Are Asking
finding: Says endorsements must be honest and not misleading and that unexpected material connections affecting evaluation should be disclosed clearly and conspicuously. It does not grant likeness permission.

publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
title: NIST AI 100-4: Reducing Risks Posed by Synthetic Content
finding: Reviews provenance, watermarking, labeling, detection, testing and auditing approaches for synthetic content. Those techniques do not establish a person’s permission by themselves.

publisher: Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity
title: C2PA Content Credentials specification 2.4
finding: Defines signed, cryptographically bound assertions about an asset’s provenance and adds repository receipts plus current soft-binding and live-video mechanisms. Validation does not decide whether a depicted person consented.
